I published my first Atlantic Canada Small-Business Opportunity Report this week.

Off-the-shelf software makes you learn its words and its process. I think there’s a better default: build the software around how the business already works.

Unpopular opinion: AI won’t take your HR job.

It takes the part you never liked: the paperwork. It drafts the letter, the reminder, the job description.

It still gets things wrong, so you check it and you decide.

The people part stays yours.

#HR #AIinHR #SmallBusiness

caption_linkedin:
Unpopular opinion: cut the job description to five requirements.

Most small-business job ads list a dozen. Half are nice-to-haves dressed up as must-haves, and good people who tick eight of them don’t apply.

Pick the five things someone truly needs on day one. Put the rest under “nice to have”. Then say the pay.

A shorter list isn’t lowering the bar. It’s telling people where the bar actually is.

#Hiring #SmallBusiness #HR
notes: No stats, no claims needing a source.

caption_linkedin:
Unpopular opinion: a reference check isn’t optional.

It’s the step that gets skipped when you’re short-staffed and the candidate interviewed well. That’s exactly when it matters.

A resume is what someone says. A reference is what someone else saw. Ask every referee the same questions, in writing, with the candidate’s consent first.

Skipping it doesn’t save the step. It just moves the surprise to week three.

#Hiring #ReferenceCheck #SmallBusiness
notes: No stats, no claims needing a source.

caption_linkedin:
Unpopular opinion: stop asking where they see themselves in five years.

For a line cook, a cleaner or a front desk agent, the honest answer is “employed, I hope”. You learn nothing, and they learn you’re reading from a list.

Ask about the job instead: “Tell me about your busiest shift. What did you do first?” Then score the answer against a guide, the same way for everyone.

Better question, same five minutes.

#Hiring #Interviewing #SmallBusiness
notes: No stats, no claims needing a source.

caption_linkedin:
Unpopular opinion: “culture fit” isn’t a hiring criterion.

It’s usually a feeling, and feelings tend to favour people who remind us of ourselves.

If you mean “shows up on time”, “stays calm on a busy Saturday” or “asks before guessing”, write that down and ask about it. Now it’s something you can score, and something every candidate gets a fair shot at.

Name the behaviour, not the vibe.

#Hiring #FairHiring #SmallBusiness

Job description of the week: dishwasher, Nova Scotia edition.

The job that keeps the kitchen open. What to put in the ad:

1. The pay. Nova Scotia’s minimum wage is $17.00 an hour since October 1, 2026. If you pay more, put the number in the ad.
2. What the shift looks like: warewashing, pots and pans, the dish machine, garbage and organics, chemicals, restocking.
3. Food hygiene. Under Nova Scotia’s Food Safety Regulations, anyone who comes into contact with food must be trained or instructed in food hygiene to a level that fits their job.
4. WHMIS. Dish machine detergent and sanitizer are hazardous products; workers who use them need WHMIS training, reviewed at least once a year.
5. Hiring a 14- or 15-year-old? They can work in a restaurant if they don’t operate cooking equipment and get proper safety training and supervision.

Job description of the week: front desk agent, Nova Scotia edition.

Check these before you post:

1. The pay. Nova Scotia’s minimum wage is $17.00 an hour since October 1, 2026. If you pay more, say how much.
2. What the shift looks like: arrivals and departures, reservations, payments, guest questions, phones, safety and the shift handover.
